Zionism and “replacement theology”
Where did Zionism come from, are the claims of Christian Zionism biblical, and is the fulfilled reading “replacement theology”?

Zionism rose from three strands: Jewish national hopes after the pogroms of the 1880s, Protestant restorationism from the 1600s, and great-power politics. Christian Zionism reads the modern state as the keeping of God's promises. The partial preterist reading answers that the promises were kept in Christ, the true Israelite, and are shared by all who are in him, Jew and Gentile. That is not replacement but fulfilment: one olive tree, from which unbelieving branches were broken and into which they can be grafted again.

What is Zionism, and how is Christian Zionism different?

Zionism is the movement for a Jewish national home in the land of Israel. Christian Zionism is the belief, held by some Christians, that supporting that state is a biblical duty because it keeps God's promises.

Political Zionism, launched by Theodor Herzl in 1896, was largely secular: a response to European antisemitism seeking a safe national home for Jews. Religious Zionism added a Jewish theological reading. Christian Zionism is older than both, rooted in 17th-century Protestant hopes of a Jewish return, and shaped in its modern form by dispensationalism. It teaches that the land promises belong to the Jewish nation today, that the state of 1948 is prophecy fulfilled, and that Christians are bound to support it. A Christian can reject Christian Zionism as a theology while loving Jewish people and supporting their safety and that of their neighbours.
Herzl's The Jewish State (1896) argued from persecution, not from Scripture.
Some strictly Orthodox Jewish groups opposed Zionism, holding that only the Messiah should bring the return.
Christian Zionist organisations such as the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem (1980) and Christians United for Israel (2006) lobby on Israel's behalf.
Christian Zionists see the return of Jews to the land after nearly two thousand years as God's hand in history, whatever the motives of the secular founders.
Why did Zionism rise in the late 19th century?
Because of persecution: the Russian pogroms of 1881-82 and the Dreyfus affair in France convinced many Jews that they would never be safe without a state of their own.

After the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in 1881, waves of violence swept Jewish communities in the Russian Empire. Leon Pinsker wrote Auto-Emancipation (1882), and the first organised settlers went to Ottoman Palestine. In Paris, the false conviction of the Jewish officer Alfred Dreyfus (1894) and the antisemitism around it moved the journalist Theodor Herzl to write The Jewish State and to call the First Zionist Congress in Basel (1897). British politicians, some raised on restorationist Bible teaching and some moved by war aims, issued the Balfour Declaration (1917). The Holocaust then made the case for a Jewish state overwhelming in many eyes.
1881-82: pogroms in the Russian Empire.
1897: First Zionist Congress, Basel.
1903: the British offer of land in East Africa was debated by the Zionist Congress and finally declined.
Christian Zionists see God's providence even in these painful causes, as he used Pharaoh and Cyrus to move his people.
What happened to the people already living in the land?
In the war of 1947-49 about 700,000 Palestinian Arabs, Muslim and Christian, fled or were driven from their homes. They remember it as the Nakba, “the catastrophe.”

The UN partition plan of November 1947 proposed Jewish and Arab states. Fighting followed, and after Israel declared independence in May 1948, neighbouring Arab states invaded. By the end of the war about 700,000 Palestinians had become refugees, and hundreds of villages were emptied. Historians still debate how much was flight and how much expulsion. Christians must hold together compassion for Jews who had just survived the Holocaust and for Palestinians, including ancient Christian communities, who lost their homes. A theology that sees only one people in the land fails the command to love our neighbour.
UN General Assembly Resolution 181 (1947): the partition plan.
Palestinian Christian families in towns like Lydda and Ramla were among those displaced.
Palestinian Christians today number in the tens of thousands in the West Bank and Gaza, and more as citizens of Israel.
Supporters of Israel stress that Arab leaders rejected partition and began the war, and that a similar number of Jews left or were expelled from Arab countries after 1948.
Was the land promise unconditional?
The promise to Abraham was certain, but living in the land was always tied to covenant faithfulness. Israel was warned it would be expelled for unfaithfulness, and it was, twice.

God swore the land to Abraham's seed, and Joshua says he kept that oath. But Moses repeatedly made staying in the land conditional: the land would vomit Israel out as it had the Canaanites if they defiled it. The exile to Babylon and then the destruction of AD 70 are those warnings carried out. The return was promised to a people who turned back to the LORD with all their heart. The unconditional heart of the promise, a seed through whom the world is blessed and an inheritance that cannot fail, is kept in Christ and widened to the whole renewed earth.
Leviticus 18:28: lest the land vomit you out when you make it unclean.
Deuteronomy 28:63-64: you shall be plucked off the land; the LORD will scatter you among all peoples.
Hebrews 11:13-16: they died not having received the things promised, seeking a better country.
Christian Zionists separate the unconditional ownership of the land from the conditional enjoyment of it: Israel could be removed for sin but never lose its title.
Will God curse nations that do not support Israel (Genesis 12:3)?
The promise was to Abraham and his seed, whom Paul names as Christ and those in him. The New Testament applies it to the blessing of the gospel, not to foreign policy.

God promised to bless those who bless Abram and curse him who dishonours him. Peter applies the promise to the sending of Jesus (Acts 3:25-26), and Paul says it was the gospel preached beforehand (Galatians 3:8-9). The people who bless Abraham's seed are those who receive Christ. Applying the verse to a modern government's policies makes political support a test of faithfulness, which Scripture never does. Christians should certainly oppose antisemitism and seek the good of Jewish people, as of all people.
Acts 3:25-26: God sent his servant to bless you by turning you from wickedness.
Galatians 3:9: those of faith are blessed along with Abraham.
The link with modern foreign policy was popularised by the Scofield Reference Bible's notes (1909).
Christian Zionists argue that the promise also covers Abraham's physical descendants, and point to the fate of empires that persecuted Jews.
Do Jewish people have their own covenant and not need Jesus?
No. Peter told the leaders of Israel there is salvation in no one else, and Paul's heart's desire was for Israel to be saved through Christ.

Some voices within or near Christian Zionism suggest that Jews are saved through God's covenant with Israel apart from faith in Jesus, or that Christians should not share the gospel with Jews. Most evangelical Christian Zionists reject this, and rightly. The apostles preached first to Jews: the gospel is the power of God for salvation, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. Jesus himself is Israel's Messiah, and to withhold him from Jewish people is the opposite of love.
Acts 4:10-12: Peter to the rulers of Israel: there is salvation in no one else.
Romans 1:16: to the Jew first.
Romans 10:1: my prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.
Dual-covenant writers appeal to Romans 11:29, that God's gifts and calling are irrevocable, and to the history of forced conversions that make evangelism of Jews painful.
Romans 11:29 says God's gifts and calling are irrevocable. Doesn't that prove Israel's national promises still stand?
It proves God has not given up on Israel: he still calls Jewish people, and they can be grafted back into their own tree by faith. It says nothing about land or a state.

Paul's point is that God's choice of Israel has not been cancelled by their present unbelief. Because of that calling, God keeps a remnant and will graft natural branches back in if they do not continue in unbelief. The calling is to Christ, and its gift is salvation. In the same chapter Paul says branches were broken off because of unbelief and stand or fall by faith. The verse is a reason to hope and pray for Jewish people to come to Jesus, not a promise of territory.
Romans 11:20: they were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith.
Romans 11:23-24: how much more will these be grafted back into their own olive tree.
Romans 11:1: I myself am an Israelite.
Christian Zionists read the irrevocable calling as including the whole package of promises given to the nation, land included.
Is the fulfilled reading “replacement theology”?
No. Replacement means God threw Israel away and chose the church instead. Fulfilment means Israel's Messiah gathered a renewed Israel around himself, Jew first, and opened the doors to the nations.

The church began as a Jewish movement: Jesus chose twelve Jewish apostles, the first thousands of believers were Jews, and Gentiles were added to them. Paul does not picture two trees, or an old tree cut down and a new one planted, but one olive tree, rooted in the patriarchs, with some branches broken off and others grafted in. Jewish believers are not replaced; they are the natural branches. So the true division is not between Israel and the church, but between those in Christ and those not yet in him. The olive-tree diagram on this page shows the three models side by side.
Acts 2:41: three thousand Jews were added in one day.
Ephesians 2:14-16: he made the two one, creating in himself one new man.
Romans 11:17: you were grafted in among the others.
Critics reply that any view denying a distinct future for ethnic Israel functions as replacement, whatever its intent.
Doesn't fulfilment theology lead to antisemitism?
Christian antisemitism is real and shameful, but it contradicts the New Testament, written almost entirely by Jews. Fulfilment theology rightly held leads to love and prayer for Jewish people.

The church's history includes terrible sins against Jews: violent sermons, expulsions, forced conversions and pogroms, and some Christians drew on theology to excuse them. Those sins must be named and repented of. But the cause was pride and hatred, which Paul specifically forbids: do not be arrogant toward the branches. Paul, who taught that believers are Abraham's seed, also said he could wish himself cut off for the sake of his people. The fulfilled reading, properly held, calls Christians to the same grief and longing.
Romans 11:18-20: do not be arrogant toward the branches; do not become proud, but fear.
Romans 9:1-3: great sorrow and unceasing anguish for my kinsmen.
Many churches have formally repented of their past teaching of contempt for Jews.
Christian Zionists argue that only an ongoing role for ethnic Israel guards fully against contempt, and point to the history of Christian antisemitism as evidence.
Does the New Testament ever call the church “Israel”?
Yes, in substance and in words: Paul blesses “the Israel of God,” Peter gives the church Israel's titles from Exodus 19, and James writes to “the twelve tribes in the dispersion.”

Paul says not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel, and that the true circumcision are those who worship by the Spirit of God. He closes Galatians with peace on all who walk by this rule, and on the Israel of God. Peter calls the scattered believers a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, the very words God spoke to Israel at Sinai, and adds Hosea's “once you were not a people.” Gentile believers were once alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, but are now fellow citizens with the saints. Each of these joins believing Gentiles to believing Israel; none excludes Jewish people.
Romans 9:6: not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel.
1 Peter 2:9-10: a holy nation, God's own people.
Ephesians 2:12, 19: no longer strangers, but fellow citizens.
Dispensationalists read “the Israel of God” as believing Jews only, and say Peter's titles describe the church by analogy without making it Israel.

This part traces how it rose, sets out the strongest claims of Christian Zionism with the partial preterist reply to each, and answers the charge that this reading is “replacement theology.” It distinguishes theology from politics: rejecting Christian Zionism as a reading of Scripture is not hostility to Jewish people, and Christians are called to love Jews and Palestinians alike.

The land belongs to the Jewish people forever by an unconditional covenant.
God alone passed between the pieces in Genesis 15, binding himself; “everlasting possession” cannot mean a temporary one.

God kept the oath (Joshua 21:43-45), but residence in the land was always conditional on faithfulness (Leviticus 18:28; Deuteronomy 28:63). The everlasting inheritance is the whole renewed earth, promised to Abraham's seed, Christ and those in him (Romans 4:13; Matthew 5:5).
Nations that bless Israel are blessed; those that oppose it are cursed.
The promise has no expiry date and history shows persecutors of Jews falling.

The New Testament applies the promise to Christ and the gospel (Acts 3:25-26; Galatians 3:8-9, 16). It is not a rule for foreign policy. Christians should oppose antisemitism because every person bears God's image.
Isaiah 66:8 was fulfilled when Israel became a nation in a day in 1948.
Israel was declared on a single day, 14 May 1948, as Isaiah foretold.

Isaiah speaks of Zion giving birth after the return from exile, with the new heavens and new earth (66:22). Paul applies Zion as mother to the Jerusalem above, mother of believers (Galatians 4:26-27). The church was born in a day at Pentecost, with three thousand added.
Ezekiel's dry bones came to life in 1948.
The bones came together first without breath: a return in unbelief, then the Spirit.

Ezekiel explains the vision: the bones are the exiles saying “our hope is lost” (37:11). The return came under Cyrus. The promised Spirit and new heart (36:26-27; 37:14) are given in the new covenant to Christ's people (2 Corinthians 3:3).
Isaiah 11:11 promises a second, worldwide return, fulfilled in modern times.
The first return was from Babylon; the second is from the four corners of the earth.

Isaiah counts the exodus from Egypt as the first time (11:16). The second is the return from Assyria, Egypt and the nations of his day. Paul quotes the same passage's root of Jesse rising to rule the nations as fulfilled in the Gentile mission (Romans 15:12).
Jerusalem must be the undivided capital of the Jewish state.
God calls Jerusalem his city and will make it a burdensome stone to all nations.

The New Testament contrasts the present Jerusalem, in slavery with her children, with the Jerusalem above, which is free (Galatians 4:25-26), and tells believers they have come to the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22). Praying for Jerusalem's peace today means praying for all its people.
A third temple must be built before Christ returns.
The man of lawlessness sits in the temple and the sacrifices must stop, so a temple must exist.

When Paul wrote, the temple stood, and he said the mystery of lawlessness was already at work. Daniel 9:27 was fulfilled when the sacrifices ended in AD 70. The New Testament never calls for a rebuilt temple; the church is God's temple (2 Corinthians 6:16).
Romans 11:26 promises the restoration of the Jewish nation in its land.
“All Israel” in verse 26 must mean ethnic Israel, contrasted with the Gentiles in verse 25.

Paul speaks of salvation by grafting into Christ, never of land or a state. Readings differ on whether “all Israel” is the whole people of God, the full Jewish remnant, or a future mass conversion, but none needs a political restoration.
If God does not keep his promises to Israel literally, how can the church trust his promises?
God ties Israel's continuance to the fixed order of the sun and moon.

God kept his promises in a greater way, as he always does: David's son reigns forever, the temple is God dwelling with his people, the land is the world. Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's new covenant as kept in Christ (Hebrews 8:8-12). Paul insists the word of God has not failed (Romans 9:6).
Israel's survival and military victories prove God's favour on the state.
The odds against Israel in 1948, 1967 and 1973 were overwhelming.
Scripture warns against reading God's approval from success (Habakkuk 1; Luke 13:1-5). Many empires won great victories. God's favour is found in Christ, not in battlefield outcomes.
Ezekiel 38-39 describes Russia and Iran invading modern Israel.
Rosh sounds like Russia, Persia is Iran, and Israel must be in the land, dwelling securely.

Rosh most likely means “chief” (“chief prince of Meshech and Tubal”). The nations named are ancient peoples around Israel. Revelation 20:8 uses Gog and Magog as a symbol for the nations gathered against the saints. Every generation has named a different invader.
The nations will be judged by how they treated the Jewish people.
“The least of these my brothers” are Jesus' Jewish brothers.
In Matthew, Jesus' brothers are his disciples: whoever does the will of my Father is my brother (Matthew 12:49-50; 28:10). The judgement concerns how people treated Christ's needy followers.
Christians have a biblical duty to give the state of Israel political support.
Gentiles owe a spiritual debt to the Jews and should repay it in material support.

Romans 15:27 is about the collection for poor Jewish believers in Jerusalem. Christians owe love to every neighbour, Jewish and Palestinian, and may judge any government's actions by God's standards of justice (Micah 6:8).
Two peoples
Israel and the church are two peoples with two programs: earthly promises for Israel, heavenly ones for the church. This is the dispensational model behind most Christian Zionism.
Paul says Christ made the two one new man, breaking down the dividing wall.
Replacement
God cut Israel off for good and planted a new, Gentile church in its place. Fulfilment theology rejects this too.
Paul says God has not rejected his people; he himself is an Israelite, and broken branches can be grafted back.
One people of God, rooted in the patriarchs. Unbelieving branches were broken off, believing Gentiles grafted in, and Jewish people welcomed back by faith. This is the fulfilment model.
Paul's own picture: one tree, one root, branches in or out by faith.
The root
The patriarchs and God's promises to them. The root supports the branches, not the other way round.
The trunk
Israel's Messiah, the true seed of Abraham, in whom the promises are kept.
Natural branches that remain
The Jewish remnant who believed: the apostles and the first thousands. They were never replaced.
Branches broken off
Those of Israel who did not believe. Broken off because of unbelief, not because of their birth.
Wild branches grafted in
Gentile believers, sharing the root's rich sap. They must not boast.
Grafted back in
Jewish people who come to faith are grafted back into their own tree, more naturally than the Gentiles.
Replacement theology is antisemitic and led to the Holocaust.
Hatred of Jews is a grievous sin that the New Testament forbids. Fulfilment theology was taught by the Jewish apostles themselves. Nazi ideology was racial and pagan, not a reading of Romans.
Theology about the promises is not hostility to people.
Critics answer that centuries of church teaching of contempt prepared the ground for the Holocaust.
It makes God unfaithful to his promises.
Paul anticipated this charge: it is not as though the word of God has failed. All the promises are yes in Christ.
Promises kept in a greater way are not promises broken.
A promise of land kept by giving something else is, to critics, not the promise made.
Romans 11:1 says God has not rejected his people.
Agreed. Paul's proof is himself and the remnant chosen by grace. Fulfilment theology affirms Israel's continuing calling to Christ.
Not rejected means a remnant now and branches regrafted, not a separate program.
Dispensationalists say the remnant is the down payment on a future national restoration.
The New Testament never calls the church Israel.
Paul blesses the Israel of God, says not all from Israel are Israel, and calls believers the true circumcision. Peter gives the church Israel's Sinai titles.
Jewish believers are Israel's core; Gentiles are joined to them.
In Paul, “Israel” usually means ethnic Israel, and Galatians 6:16 may mean believing Jews.
It spiritualises the plain meaning of the prophets.
The apostles read the prophets this way first: James on Amos 9, Hebrews on Jeremiah 31, Paul on Hosea. Typology follows real history to its fulfilment; it is not allegory.
Following the New Testament's own reading is not allegory.
Dispensationalists hold that the New Testament applies these texts without cancelling their original meaning for Israel.
It began with Augustine and the imperial church.
Justin taught that the church is the true Israel around AD 155, long before Constantine, and the idea comes from Jesus and Paul.
Early writers on both sides of the millennium held it.
Critics answer that the early church's growing hostility to Judaism shaped how it read these texts.
Jeremiah 31:35-37 says Israel will never cease to be a nation.
The promise comes with the new covenant, which Hebrews says is kept in Christ. Israel has never ceased: its remnant lives on in Christ's people, with Jewish believers in every generation.
The continuing Israel is the believing Israel of the new covenant.
Critics argue “nation” must mean the ethnic people, who have survived as a people against all odds.
God's gifts and calling are irrevocable.
That is why Jewish people are still called and can be grafted back by faith. The calling is to Christ, not to territory.
Irrevocable calling, conditional branches.
Christian Zionists read the calling as including all the national promises.
It makes Gentile Christians arrogant toward Jews.
Paul forbids exactly that pride. The fulfilled reading, rightly held, calls Gentiles to humility, gratitude and longing for Israel's salvation.
Humility is part of the doctrine, not an add-on.
History shows the doctrine has often been held with pride.
Revelation 7 lists the tribes, so ethnic Israel has a future role.

John hears the number of the tribes, then sees a great multitude from every nation, as he heard of a lion and saw a lamb (5:5-6). The list is irregular: Dan is missing, Joseph and Manasseh both appear. It pictures the whole people of God as Israel's army.
John's hearing-then-seeing pattern joins the two groups.
Futurists see two distinct groups: a Jewish remnant sealed on earth and a Gentile multitude in heaven.
Jesus said Jerusalem would see him again when it says “Blessed is he who comes.”
The saying is conditional: Jerusalem would not see him until it welcomed him. It promises nothing about a state. Many fulfilled readers welcome a future turning of Jews to Christ.
A hope of conversion, not of restoration to the land.
Dispensationalists read it as a prophecy of national repentance at the return.
“All Israel will be saved” proves a national future.
Even if it means a future mass conversion, as many Reformed and postmillennial writers hold, it is salvation in Christ within the one olive tree, not a separate covenant or a land promise.
A future for Jewish people in Christ is part of fulfilment theology.
Dispensationalists link the salvation to the restored nation at Christ's return.
